title: Discover 9 Surprising Hollywood Secrets, Including 'Poltergeist' Using Real Skeletons
byline: ParadeFollowMorgan MurrellAdd to Preferred SourcesThu, October 8, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
excerpt: A roundup of behind-the-scenes facts about some of Hollywood's most popular movies and celebrities.
content:
Some of Hollywood's latest and greatest projects were brought together by accidents on set, improvised lines, and unconventional bonding between co-stars. That's what makes films and TV shows so interesting, because the magic behind the scenes is what truly brings these stories to life. Here are some unique Hollywood facts you should know about Poltergeist, Danny DeVito, The Godfather, and more:

Pierce Brosnan was forbidden from wearing traditional tuxedos outside of his James Bond films.
According to Collider, Brosnan was contractually prohibited from wearing them in any other movie while part of the iconic secret agent franchise. Tuxedos were a staple of the character, so the studio didn't want his formal attire to be associated with anything else he worked on. He actively played 007 from 1995 to 2002. The restriction became noticeable to the public when he starred in 1999's The Thomas Crown Affair and wore a midnight blue dinner suit, with an open white shirt and a white (untied) bow tie to a black-and-white-themed ball. According to commentary from director John McTiernan on the film's DVD, he confirmed that Brosnan's Bond contract caused his unconventional look during that scene.

Steve Buscemi used to be a New York City firefighter.
In a 2021 op-ed for Time Magazine, the Golden Globe Award-winning actor spoke candidly about his time as a first responder for Engine 55 in Lower Manhattan. At the time, he was trying to juggle working as a firefighter while also taking acting classes. Once he began booking movies and plays, Buscemi took a leave of absence. He returned as a volunteer on 9/11.
"After four years on the job, it became impossible to juggle my shifts with both a movie and a play," Buscemi wrote. "I took a leave of absence, figuring I'd be back. Seventeen years later, I was. One of the strongest sensations that flooded over me on Sept. 11, 2001, was that feeling of connection. The next morning, I grabbed my old gear, got a lift to the site, and found a place on a bucket brigade."

Tony Todd was paid every time a bee stung him in Candyman.
More than 200,000 real honeybees were used in the 1992 horror film Candyman. Although the bees were managed by a specialist, Todd knew anything could happen when it came to these insects. So, he negotiated a special clause in his contract that would ensure he was paid an extra $1,000 for every bee sting he endured while filming. During that iconic scene where bees emerge from his mouth, Todd wore a protective mouthpiece to keep the bees from going down his throat. About 500 bees were placed in his mouth, and it took nearly 30 minutes to get them out. Despite the protection, Todd was reportedly stung over 20 times, resulting in a hefty bonus of more than $20,000.

Cindy Crawford studied chemical engineering before becoming an established model.
After graduating as valedictorian of DeKalb High School in Illinois in 1984, Crawford earned a full academic scholarship to study chemical engineering at Northwestern University. With the demands of her growing modeling career increasing, it became difficult to balance her college classes. Crawford dropped out after one semester, moved to New York, and became a full-time model.

Marlon Brando's cat scene in The Godfather wasn't scripted.
Brando's performance as Vito Corleone in The Godfather is probably one of his most talked-about performances to date. During the opening scene, Brando's character is seen with a cat on his lap to show a glaring contrast between his gentle demeanor and a chilling conversation about murder. Turns out, the cat wasn't originally in the film. Director Francis Ford Coppola found the stray cat wandering around the Paramount Pictures studio lot. Coppola handed Brando the cat to see what would happen and it turned into cinematic gold.

Danny DeVito and Michael Douglas were roommates.
Now household names in Hollywood, DeVito and Douglas became roommates in NYC when they were both struggling actors in the late 1960s. The two initially met as acting students at the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Connecticut, working in summer stock theater. They bonded while smoking marijuana. They'd reconnect a couple of years later in New York, ultimately becoming roommates. They'd go on to collaborate on some major projects together, including One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Romancing the Stone. They're still super close friends.

Real human skeletons were used in 1982's Poltergeist.
The film's climax scene features Diane Freeling falling into an unfinished pool, only to find she's not the only one in it. The character becomes surrounded by skeletons as she desperately tries to escape. Turns out, due to the production team's budget, they found out that it was cheaper to buy authentic skeletons versus manufactured plastic props. But don't worry, no graves were robbed during this process. They were acquired legally through an international educational collection.
JoBeth Williams, who played Diane, didn't find out they were real until after filming took place. She spent days submerged in muddy water surrounded by the real deal. "If I'd known the skeletons were real, I'd have been even more disgusted," Williams said, per The Guardian.

Matthew Perry is missing the tip of one finger.
Due to an unfortunate accident during his toddler years, the late Friends star is missing the tip of the middle finger on his right hand. His finger was slammed in a door when he was just three years old.

Christopher Nolan planted 500 acres of corn to avoid using CGI in Interstellar.
To ensure Cooper's farm drone chase scene was as authentic as possible, Nolan decided to grow real corn outside of Calgary, Canada. Despite risking crop failure and unpredictable weather, the idea worked. It cost about $100,000 to plant and manage the corn. When filming wrapped, production harvested and sold the crops, which generated about $162,000.
